claims.text: High-temperature wear resistance of an FeNiCrCoCu thin coating is governed by in situ formation of a stable, adherent oxide layer.
The oxide layer acts as a lubricious barrier during wear.
The oxide layer develops at elevated temperatures.
Oxide-layer formation reduces friction relative to an unoxidized condition.
Oxide-layer formation reduces mass loss relative to an unoxidized condition.
Elevated-temperature oxidation of FeNiCrCoCu produces a protective oxide scale.
The oxide film reduces direct metal-to-metal contact during sliding.
The oxide film limits wear by acting as a barrier to further oxidation or material removal.
A continuous, adherent mixed-metal oxide layer forms on the FeNiCrCoCu coating surface.
Pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have a lower high-temperature friction coefficient than as-deposited coatings.
Pre-oxidized FeNiCrCoCu coatings will have a lower high-temperature wear rate or mass loss than as-deposited coatings.
Emergence of oxide phases during in situ oxidation will coincide with improved tribological performance.
Oxide formation is minimal for an as-deposited FeNiCrCoCu coating tested at room temperature and low applied loads.
The proposed oxide-mediated wear benefit applies in ambient air at temperatures up to 800 degrees Celsius.
The proposed effect applies under loads typical of industrial high-temperature wear conditions.
The proposed mechanism may not apply in inert atmospheres.
The proposed mechanism may fail when oxidation kinetics are too slow or when the oxide scale spalls.
A lack of significant friction and wear reduction after pre-oxidation or in situ oxidation would falsify the hypothesis.
Failure to detect an adherent oxide layer correlated with improved wear resistance would falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The stated baseline is an as-deposited coating tested at room temperature and low load, whereas the proposed comparison tests both as-deposited and pre-oxidized coatings across temperatures up to 800 degrees Celsius. This leaves it unclear whether the intended control is a room-temperature baseline or an as-deposited coating tested at the same high temperature and load.

The hypothesis contrasts oxidized material with an unoxidized as-deposited condition, but an as-deposited specimen heated in ambient air during the proposed test may oxidize in situ. Thus, the nominal control may not remain unoxidized.
